name: Oral contraceptives for hair

card.summary: Combined hormonal pills with anti-androgenic progestins are used in some women to lower androgen activity, which can reduce excess facial/body hair and support treatment of androgen-related hair thinning.
card.note: Prescription only; carries a small clotting risk and is not suitable for everyone.

quick.overview:
Combined oral contraceptive pills contain an estrogen and a progestin. In women whose hair or skin concerns are driven by androgens, such as excess facial hair (hirsutism) or acne, doctors may prescribe pills with anti-androgenic progestins to bring those hormones down.

The appearance payoff is mainly less unwanted hair and clearer skin; for androgen-related hair thinning, the pill is described as one option that may help in some women, often alongside other treatments. Evidence comes from dermatology and gynaecology rather than from looksmaxxing communities.
quick.how: The pill is prescribed and taken by mouth as directed by a clinician. Doctors choose among formulations; those with progestins such as drospirenone or cyproterone acetate are described as anti-androgenic. Effects on hair are gradual and typically assessed over months.
quick.risks: All combined pills slightly raise the risk of venous blood clots, with figures varying by progestin; other effects and contraindications are assessed by the prescriber. It is prescription-only and not a treatment for male-pattern hair loss.

lead: Combined oral contraceptive pills pair an estrogen with a progestin. Wikipedia reports that they are used to treat androgen-driven conditions including acne and hirsutism, and that for women with polycystic ovary syndrome who also have androgenic alopecia they can help those symptoms.[1]

The mechanism described is that the estrogen reduces ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone-binding globulin, lowering free testosterone.[1] Progestins differ: levonorgestrel, norgestimate and desogestrel are classed as androgenic, while cyproterone acetate, drospirenone and dienogest are antiandrogenic.[1]

For female pattern hair loss, treatments highlighted in Wikipedia include minoxidil, antiandrogens such as spironolactone, laser therapy and transplantation; its treatment section does not discuss contraceptives specifically.[2]

chain: Pill raises SHBG and reduces ovarian androgens
Less excess facial/body hair, clearer skin, possible support for androgenic thinning
angle.text: By lowering androgen activity, anti-androgenic pills can reduce hormone-driven hair growth in unwanted places and are used alongside other treatments in androgen-related hair thinning in some women.

paras: Combined pills treat hirsutism and acne, and are preferred in PCOS when acne, hirsutism or androgenic alopecia are present because they can improve those symptoms.[1]
Estrogen suppresses ovarian androgen production and increases SHBG, reducing free testosterone and sebum production.[1]

All combined pill users have a small increase in venous thromboembolism risk, about 60 versus 30 per 100,000 woman-years in non-users, with variation by progestin.[1] Wikipedia reports that the FDA found higher VTE risk with drospirenone pills in the first year compared with other pills.[1]
The topic is rare in looksmaxxing forums, which are mostly male; mentions on T Nation relate to PCOS, metformin and general hormone risks rather than hair loss specifically.
No studies found specifically on hair-loss use here; the effects on acne and hirsutism are summarised in Wikipedia's review of combined pills.[1]
